title: ESG Ratings Disagree
text: ESG Ratings Disagree 3 Five raters: KLD, Sustainalytics, Vigeo-Eiris, RobecoSAM and Asset4, on a common sample of firms The correlation: 0.61 on average, and from 0.42 to 0.73 across the ten pairs of raters Credit ratings: Moody's and Standard and Poor's correlate at 0.99 The dimensions: agreement is lowest on social and governance scores Berg, Koelbel and Rigobon (2019), MIT Sloan Working Paper 5822-19, Table 2, page 7; credit-rating correlation from page 2. Averages are computed from the table.

title: Sources of Rating Divergence
text: Sources of Rating Divergence 4 Measurement: the same category is scored differently, 53 per cent of the divergence Scope: raters cover different categories, 44 per cent Weight: raters weight categories differently, 3 per cent Water: all five raters score it, and the scores correlate at 0.33 on average Berg, Koelbel and Rigobon (2019), MIT Sloan Working Paper 5822-19, pages 3 to 4 (decomposition) and page 18 (Table 5, water category). Regression-based decomposition.

title: Climate Risk in Long-Dated Asset Prices
text: Climate Risk in Long-Dated Asset Prices 5 Giglio, Kelly and Stroebel (2020), NBER Working Paper 28226, pages 7 to 9, 16, 22 and 23. Bernstein and co-authors, Painter and Goldsmith-Pinkham and co-authors are reported through the survey. Asset Evidence Size What it shows Coastal homes Bernstein and co-authors (2019) 14.7 per cent discount at one foot of sea-level rise; 13.8 at two to three feet; 4.4 at six feet Exposed homes sell below equivalent unexposed homes Municipal bonds Painter (2020); Goldsmith-Pinkham and co-authors (2019) Present value of long-run cash flows 3 to 8 per cent lower The yield effect sits in long-dated bonds and is absent at short maturities Discount rates Giglio, Kelly and Stroebel (2020) Sign of the risk premium on climate hedges is disputed Negative if the uncertainty is about climate, positive if it is about the economy

title: Water Risk Indicators
text: Water Risk Indicators 6 Thirteen indicators in three groups, covering quantity, quality and reputational risk, are combined into one overall score. Each is assigned a risk element, hazard, exposure or vulnerability, and risk is their product. Kuzma and co-authors (2023), Aqueduct 4.0, WRI Technical Note, August 2023, pages 1 to 2, 10 and 11. Thresholds from Aqueduct 2.1 (Gassert and co-authors, 2014). Baseline water stress, demand as a share of supply Risk category Score Below 10 per cent Low 0 to 1 10 to 20 per cent Low-medium 1 to 2 20 to 40 per cent Medium-high 2 to 3 40 to 80 per cent High 3 to 4 Above 80 per cent Extremely high 4 to 5

title: The Cost of Disrupted Infrastructure
text: The Cost of Disrupted Infrastructure 7 The cost of disruption: at least USD 390 billion a year to households and firms in low and middle income countries The cost of resilience: 3 per cent added to investment needs in new infrastructure The return: USD 4 of benefit for each dollar, USD 4.2 trillion over the life of new assets The spread: the ratio is above 6 in a quarter of 3,000 scenarios and above 1 in 96 per cent Hallegatte, Rentschler and Rozenberg (2019), Lifelines: The Resilient Infrastructure Opportunity, World Bank, Overview, pages vii and 12. Pre-publication overview booklet.

title: The Carbon Premium in Stock Returns
text: The Carbon Premium in Stock Returns 8 The premium: firms with higher emissions earn higher returns, after the usual controls The size: one standard deviation of scope 1 adds 1.8 per cent a year, and of scope 3 adds 4.0 per cent Intensity: emission intensity, the usual screening measure, has no significant effect Timing: no premium appears in the 1990s, so awareness matters Bolton and Kacperczyk (2020), NBER Working Paper 26968, pages 1 and 6 to 8, and Table 8 discussion, page 18. Annualised effect of a one-standard-deviation increase.

title: The Green Bond Premium
text: The Green Bond Premium 9 The framework: assets that give a nonpecuniary benefit are priced at a premium Green municipal bonds: about 6 basis points lower yield, 0.6 percentage points of value at a ten-year duration Certified green: 26 basis points lower in the first specification and 15 with issuer fixed effects Ownership: green bonds are more closely held than ordinary bonds Baker, Bergstresser, Serafeim and Wurgler (2018), NBER Working Paper 25194, pages 1 to 3, 17 and 18. After-tax yield at issue, US municipal bonds.

title: Climate-Related Disclosure: Four Pillars
text: Climate-Related Disclosure: Four Pillars 10 Transition risks are policy and legal, technology, market and reputation. Physical risks are acute, event-driven, or chronic, longer-term shifts. Water availability, sourcing and quality are named among the physical effects. Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (2017), Final Report, June 2017, Figure 4, page 14, and pages 5 and 6. Wording shortened. Governance Strategy Risk management Metrics and targets Board oversight of risks and opportunities Risks and opportunities over the short, medium and long term Processes for identifying and assessing risks Metrics used to assess risks and opportunities Management's role in assessing and managing them Impact on business, strategy and financial planning Processes for managing risks Scope 1, scope 2 and, if appropriate, scope 3 emissions Resilience of the strategy under scenarios, including 2 degrees Celsius or lower Integration into overall risk management Targets and performance against them

title: Water as a Financial Stability Risk
text: Water as a Financial Stability Risk 11 Banco de España (2026), press release of 20 May 2026, an announcement of the agenda and not a report of conclusions. Jobst, A. (2026), Scaling Water Resilience in Finance: Policy, Practice and Action, UNEP FI and OECD programme proposal, draft V.04.04.2026, pages 1 to 8, plans as at April 2026. NGFS membership page, 26 August 2026. The meeting: 21 and 22 May 2026 at the Banco de España, convened by the OECD, the NGFS and CDP The risk: macroeconomic and financial risks from water scarcity, variability and quality The agenda: sectoral vulnerabilities, sovereign exposure, price stability, supervisory responses and insurance protection gaps The aim: to advance understanding of water as a systemic financial stability risk The programme: Scaling Water Resilience in Finance, run by UNEP FI and the OECD, plans a central bank joint statement drafted through the NGFS (152 members) and a showcase of market practice

title: The Programme: Two Planned Outputs and a Timeline
text: The Programme: Two Planned Outputs and a Timeline 12 Jobst, A. (2026), Scaling Water Resilience in Finance: Policy, Practice and Action, UNEP FI and OECD programme proposal, draft V.04.04.2026, pages 4 to 6. Plans as at April 2026, not outcomes. Joint statement on water risk in financial supervision Water risk practice showcase What it is A statement drafted by central banks through the NGFS, extending climate and nature approaches to freshwater A curated showcase of how banks, insurers, investors and rating agencies already handle water risk What it is not A commitment to any supervision, or a replacement for climate and nature frameworks A compact, a requirement to change methods, or a supervisory expectation Who endorses or contributes Central banks and supervisors, NGFS members, regional leaders including the UAE Central Bank Insurers, rating agencies, banks, investors and development finance institutions Timing Drafted in Q3 2026, published in Q4 2026 Curated in Q3 2026, launched in Q4 2026 After that 2027: OECD-led roundtables on supporting uptake by supervisors 2027: continued engagement through UNEP FI and OECD platforms

title: Data Centres and Environmental Damages
text: Data Centres and Environmental Damages 13 The estimate: 250 TWh in 2025, 5 to 6 per cent of US generation, and USD 25 billion of damages, within a range of USD 10 to 33 billion The incidence: Texas and Virginia bear 30 per cent of the total The comparison: 5 per cent of industry GDP overall, and more than industry GDP in North Dakota and Wyoming The valuation: carbon at USD 190 a tonne, or USD 50 in the alternative Muller (2026), NBER Working Paper 35100, April 2026, abstract and Table 2. Gross external damages divided by state GDP of data processing, hosting and related services.

title: Flexible Data Centres and the Grid
text: Flexible Data Centres and the Grid 14 The baseline: load growth to 2030 raises CO2 by 20, 58 and 24 per cent in the three regions The cost: flexible load lowers system costs by up to 4, 5 and 2 per cent The emissions: up to 40 per cent lower in Texas, up to 3 per cent higher elsewhere The condition: the advantage disappears where renewables are dear Knittel, Senga and Wang (2025), NBER Working Paper 34065, July 2025, pages 1 to 3, 8 and 12. Model of three US systems in 2030; 'at most' values from the scenarios.

title: Three Models for Long-Lived Assets
text: Three Models for Long-Lived Assets 15 Each page opens on a generic setting. The case supplies the evidence to test them. Pastor, Stambaugh and Taylor (2021); HM Treasury (2026); Freeman and Groom (2026); author's calculation. Interactive pages in web/. Topic Model Prediction Page The price of sustainability Pastor, Stambaugh and Taylor (2021) Greener assets cost more and earn less; investors who care give up return Pricing sustainability preferences The value of a distant benefit Green Book (2026), June 2026 review, gamma discounting The schedule decides what a century of benefit is worth Discounting long-lived assets The payoff to protection Expected annual loss with a protection standard Net benefit peaks at a standard that moves with climate and discounting The payoff to resilience

title: Pastor, Stambaugh and Taylor (2021): Tastes and Prices
text: Pastor, Stambaugh and Taylor (2021): Tastes and Prices 16 The setting: investors gain a nonpecuniary benefit from green holdings, in proportion to their taste The price: expected return is the CAPM return less the average taste over risk aversion, times the ESG score The portfolios: above-average investors tilt green, below-average investors tilt brown The condition: if everyone has the same taste, all hold the market and the alphas remain Pastor, Stambaugh and Taylor (2021), Journal of Financial Economics 142(2), 550–571; NBER Working Paper 26549, equations 4 to 10 and 14, pages 6 to 11.

title: The Price of a Preference
text: The Price of a Preference 17 The alpha: minus 48 basis points a year on the greener asset and plus 48 on the browner one The give-up: ESG-minded investors earn 16 basis points a year less than the market The gain: indifferent investors earn 7 basis points more The dispersion: the give-up is largest at equal wealth and zero when tastes are the same Author's calculation from Pastor, Stambaugh and Taylor (2021), NBER Working Paper 26549, equations 9, 10 and 14; illustrative inputs (models_w7.py).

title: The Treasury Discount Rate and Its Schedules
text: The Treasury Discount Rate and Its Schedules 18 An uncertain rate with a gamma distribution gives a forward rate that starts at the mean and falls with the horizon. The review is independent and is not Treasury policy. HM Treasury (2026), Green Book supplementary guidance: discounting, Tables 3.A and 3.B, pages 12 and 13; Freeman and Groom (2026), Table 1, page 2 of 15. Forward rate, per cent Years 1 to 30 Years 31 to 75 Years 76 to 125 Green Book, February 2026 3.5 3.0 2.5 Green Book, no pure time preference 3.00 2.57 2.14 Review, June 2026, standard projects 3.0 2.5 2.25 Review, June 2026, social insurance projects 1.5 1.0 0.75

title: The Value of a Distant Benefit
text: The Value of a Distant Benefit 19 The range: 100 received in year 100 is worth 3.2 at a flat 3.5 per cent and 33.9 on the social insurance schedule The Treasury: 5.1 on the Green Book schedule The uncertain rate: 14.9 with a mean of 3 per cent and a standard deviation of 2 A level stream: a benefit-cost ratio from 1.5 to 2.4, a spread of 1.6, against 10.6 for the distant amount Author's calculation from HM Treasury (2026), Tables 3.A and 3.B, and Freeman and Groom (2026), Table 1; gamma regime derived (models_w7.py). Illustrative project.

title: Expected Annual Loss and Protection
text: Expected Annual Loss and Protection 20 The curve: loss from an event with a return period of T years is the 100-year loss times (T/100) to the power s Expected loss: the area under loss against annual probability Protection: a standard of R years removes the losses of every event up to R Drift: frequency and exposed value grow, so avoided loss rises over the years The appraisal: discount the avoided losses and compare them with cost and upkeep Author's model (models_w7.py). Risk as hazard, exposure and vulnerability from Kuzma and co-authors (2023), Aqueduct 4.0, pages 10 and 11; benefit-cost range from Hallegatte, Rentschler and Rozenberg (2019), page 12.

title: Choosing a Protection Standard
text: Choosing a Protection Standard 21 The loss: a one-in-100-year event costs 100 million and a one-in-1,000-year event 316 million The payoff: expected annual loss of 13.5 million, of which a one-in-50 standard avoids 11.3 million The result: benefit-cost ratio of 2.8 and net present value of 259 million, with the best standard about one in 29 The sensitivity: a heavy tail and fast drift move the best standard to about one in 67 Author's model (models_w7.py); illustrative inputs. Risk elements from Kuzma and co-authors (2023), Aqueduct 4.0; benefit-cost range from Hallegatte, Rentschler and Rozenberg (2019), Overview, page 12.

title: Three Models Compared
text: Three Models Compared 22 Pastor, Stambaugh and Taylor (2021); Baker and co-authors (2018); Berg, Koelbel and Rigobon (2019); HM Treasury (2026); Freeman and Groom (2026); Hallegatte, Rentschler and Rozenberg (2019), page 12.
